title: Air Force Tells Congress It Needs 1,509 Fighters by 2035 — and Bets $2.34B on a Reconciliation Bill That Hasn't Passed
subhead: A new Air Force force-structure report sets a 1,509 combat-coded fighter target for 2035 with F-35s at 40% of the fleet, but the buy depends on a reconciliation package still stuck in the Senate. Meanwhile Europe moves to hand utilities the legal power to shoot down drones, and Germany raises its sabotage threat level to the second-highest tier.

sections.heading: The Air Force's 1,509-Fighter Plan — and the $2.34 Billion Hole Under It
sections.body:
The U.S. Air Force sent Congress a force-structure report on Oct. 16 concluding it needs 1,509 combat-coded fighters by 2035, according to Defense News. Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, briefed reporters on the report at a Pentagon roundtable Oct. 20; reporters were not given a copy.

The mix Tabor described: F-35s at about 40% of the fleet (up from roughly 30% today), F-22s and their replacement F-47 at about 20% combined, with F-15s and F-16s splitting the remaining 40% about evenly. A-10s are not in the 2035 plan. The service intends to replace its F-22s with roughly the same number of F-47s.

The target assumes medium risk — the second of four risk tiers, where forces likely achieve their objectives but could strain in prolonged operations. Tabor said the analysis predates this year's Iran war and was not driven by it.

The funding is the weak point. The Air Force has long said it needs 72 fighters a year; the FY27 request seeks 38 F-35s and 24 F-15EXs — 62 total. Of the 38 F-35s, $2.34 billion covering 14 aircraft rides on a reconciliation bill that can clear the Senate with a simple majority. If it fails, Tabor said the service would either pull money from other programs or push those buys into 2028. Multiyear contracts for the F-35 and F-15EX are pending in Congress; Tabor argued they would give Lockheed Martin and Boeing stability to expand output, and said industry has 'assured us that they can' deliver.

Notably, the 1,509 figure excludes Collaborative Combat Aircraft. The Air Force plans 500 CCAs by 2032, but Tabor said drones are not yet changing the crewed fighter requirement — though they could reduce it in future reports.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first explicit statement that the Air Force's crewed-fighter requirement will not shrink even as it fields 500 wingman drones — a deliberate hedge that autonomy is not yet trusted to substitute for airframes. The reconciliation dependency also means the actual fleet size is being decided by a budget maneuver, not by military analysis.

sections.heading: A Framework, Not a Contract: Pentagon Locks In 25,000 APKWS Kits a Year
sections.body:
The Department of War signed a framework agreement with BAE Systems for up to 25,000 APKWS guidance kits per year for as long as seven years, the department announced Monday. APKWS converts unguided 2.75-inch rockets into laser-guided munitions — and has become the Pentagon's preferred cheap answer to drones, since all four services field it.

Three caveats matter. Congress still has to approve and fund the buy. Neither side disclosed the cost. And this is a framework, not a contract — the multiyear contract is still being negotiated. The framework outlines a path to 35,000 kits a year for allies as partner nations request kits through Foreign Military Sales.

Undersecretary for acquisition and sustainment Michael Duffey framed it as 'flipping the cost calculus in the taxpayer's favor.' BAE builds the kits in Hudson, New Hampshire, and Austin, Texas, and delivered its 100,000th kit in February. The existing Navy five-year contract, awarded August 2025, is worth up to $1.74 billion for up to 55,000 kits through December 2031. Allied demand is already visible: Saudi Arabia won State Department approval in July for a possible $1.96 billion package including up to 20,000 kits, and Italy is weighing 5,031 for counter-drone defense.

It slots into a year of framework deals: Lockheed Martin's January agreement to more than triple PAC-3 MSE production, BAE and Lockheed's March deal to quadruple THAAD seekers, and a June THAAD interceptor contract worth more than $35 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is now using multiyear demand commitments — not annual appropriations — as its industrial policy instrument across interceptors, seekers and now rocket guidance kits. The risk is that frameworks are promises, and if Congress does not fund them, industry has committed capacity it cannot staff.

sections.heading: Europe's Drone Defense Problem Is Legal, Not Technical
sections.body:
Reuters reporting carried by Defense News lays out a widening gap: the technology to detect and bring down drones is maturing faster than the rules on who may use it. At a former flight-test base at Brétigny-sur-Orge south of Paris, jammers and interceptor drones are being evaluated for clients that are increasingly not governments — utilities, rail operators and other critical-infrastructure firms that want to shoot drones down themselves.

France moved first: parliament passed a law in August allowing approved critical-infrastructure operators and contractors to detect, jam and shoot down drones near designated facilities. The law responded partly to drone flights over the Ile Longue nuclear submarine base near Brest in December 2025. Paris wants an expanded list of sensitive sites equipped by 2027. Systematic Paris-Region, which runs the Brétigny testing program, said evaluations launched this summer have catalogued three systems integrators and 17 counter-drone systems so far.

Poland has gone furthest operationally — operators have deployed counter-drone systems, trained with military and police, and established drone-restricted zones around energy infrastructure, with designated security units authorized to destroy, disable or take control of intruding drones. Austria announced similar plans in September; Defense Minister Klaudia Tanner said the state cannot protect every site. In Germany, counter-drone operations remain a policing function and the interior ministry says it is reviewing how operators could be legally involved.

The unresolved issue is liability. Two sources at energy transmission companies on NATO's eastern flank told Reuters that without assurances — or a judicial precedent — on who bears responsibility for collateral damage, operators will stay reluctant to act. E.ON CEO Leonhard Birnbaum said operators must assume some attacks will succeed rather than plan to stop all of them; the company runs about 2,720 substations in Germany. Eurelectric's Kristian Ruby warned of a real possibility of heating outages this winter from hybrid attacks.
sections.whyItMatters: The binding constraint on European counter-drone defense is not procurement but legal authority and liability allocation. That is a slower thing to fix than a system buy — and large transformers take years to replace, so a single successful strike has an outsized cost.

sections.heading: Bundeswehr Raises Sabotage Threat to Second-Highest Level Over Wunstorf Drone
sections.body:
Germany's military raised its assessment of the Russian sabotage threat to its second-highest level, warning that Bundeswehr forces themselves could be attacked at home, according to a classified internal analysis reported by WDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung on Oct. 21. An Operational Command spokesperson told WDR the risk is now rated 'substantial.'

The trigger was the September discovery of an apparently crashed drone near Wunstorf air base in northern Germany, with a can containing explosives found a few meters away. Federal Criminal Police Office technical analysis suggests the drone may have lain near the base for about two years, and its construction resembled the explosives-laden drone used in the failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August.

The analytical distinction is the important part. Leipzig targeted Ukrainian aircraft — an indirect threat to German forces. Wunstorf is assessed as likely targeting Bundeswehr aircraft themselves. The analysis concludes Russia almost certainly has the capability and very likely an increased motivation to act against German forces and facilities, and that Moscow's use of armed drones crossed a previously anticipated threshold involving intent to cause physical damage or lethal effects.

Previous German assessments had centered on a narrow set of sites: installations training Ukrainian troops, naval bases and shipyards. The new one says vulnerable sites can no longer be geographically confined — an all-around deterioration with concrete actions possible in the near term. The report follows suspicious drone flights over sites tied to Germany's Arrow 3 missile-defense system and Patriot maintenance facilities. Russia denies involvement and has called the Leipzig allegations a 'provocation.'
sections.whyItMatters: The shift from site-specific to nationwide threat assessment changes what German force protection has to buy and where it has to garrison. It also confirms that Russia's campaign is aimed at the German military-industrial and training pipeline, not just Ukrainian targets on German soil.

sections.heading: China's Planners Are Reading the Marine Corps Strategy — and Writing Their Own Answer
sections.body:
An analysis by Lyle Goldstein (Brown University's Watson School, Defense Priorities) in Defense News surveys recent Chinese-language assessments of the USMC's 2019 dispersed-operations strategy — and finds a response that is more forward-leaning than defensive.

Chinese naval magazine Modern Ships noted with alarm that the Marines are experimenting with unmanned surface vessels able to fire the stealthy LRASM anti-ship cruise missile, but flagged weaknesses including sensor and drone range limits and 'precarious' air defense. A 2026 study in the navy-affiliated Shipborne Weapons argued the Marine Littoral Regiments 'actually represent campaign preparation by the USMC to militarily intervene in China's unification,' and concluded the strategy is vulnerable because the U.S. 'has no way to quickly establish air superiority.'

The most significant piece — written by senior active-duty Chinese Navy officers, originally in an internal-circulation journal, and translated by the U.S. Naval War College's China Maritime Studies Institute — describes the new USMC deployments as 'continuous penetration and encroachment into our near seas.' It argues China must 'establish effective countermeasures' through a 'proactive offensive posture,' extending undersea combat capability 'as far forward as feasible.' It also notes forward Marines could deploy hydro-acoustic arrays to track Chinese submarines and drone swarms 'to overwhelm our radar tracking capacity.'

The Global Times has separately pushed back on Japan's disclosure of six PLA movement reports in two days — including the Liaoning carrier group training in far seas and the large U.S.-Japan Keen Sword 27 exercise — calling the reporting alarmism meant to justify Japan's own buildup.
sections.whyItMatters: Chinese naval officers are explicitly framing forward-deployed USMC units as an offensive problem requiring forward Chinese counter-deployment. That is the security dilemma operating in plain text — and it suggests the Marine Littoral Regiment concept may be generating exactly the escalation it was meant to deter.

sections.heading: Golden Dome Gets an Army Unit but Still Not a Budget
sections.body:
Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, commanding general of Army Space and Missile Defense Command, confirmed at AUSA that an Army air defense unit has been 'earmarked' for Golden Dome support — a unit he declined to identify, describing it as 'a well-trained organization that we know can meet the demands.' Rafferty framed GDA as disaggregating current aggregated sensor-interceptor-C2 packages so commanders can pair 'any sensor, best shooter, right C2' across the country.

Joint Task Force Gold — a 100-person unit under U.S. Northern Command, led by Army officers and established in January — has run planning 'sprints' since February with about 300 members of the GDA stakeholder community in Colorado Springs. Deputy commander Col. Kevin Stonerook said the next sprint is set for the end of October and that the task force is assembling a cyber warfare capability and helping site the system. 'There's a lot we still have to figure out,' he said.

The money remains the problem. The Pentagon requested $17.5 billion for Golden Dome in FY27 through a $350 billion reconciliation package, with only about $400 million in R&D in the base budget. Air & Space Forces Magazine reported in September that a dispute over the reconciliation bill could leave the bulk of funding in jeopardy. Officials want an early version fielded by the end of next year and a fuller system by 2035; lawmakers of both parties have complained about slow progress and inconsistent White House communication.
sections.whyItMatters: The Army is organizing people and command structures for a program whose funding is still contingent on the same reconciliation bill the Air Force's fighter buy depends on. Two of the Pentagon's largest modernization bets now share a single legislative failure point.

sections.heading: Smaller Signals: Army Network Funding, CCA-Ready Maven, CSTO Arms to Tajikistan
sections.body:
NGC2 funding uncertainty. Lt. Gen. Matt McFarlane, commander of I Corps, said Oct. 13 that fielding the Army's Next Generation Command and Control system across the formation by the end of FY27 'is based on resources available — that's not in my job jar.' The Army's FY27 request includes $904 million for NGC2 R&D and scaling, and Anduril holds a contract worth up to $1.8 billion for the common data baseline. Congress is in recess, leaving the NDAA timeline murky (Defense News).

Maven goes service-wide in the Marine Corps. The service made its AI-enabled battlefield management system available to all commands and organizations, per Defense News — the clearest sign yet that the Pentagon's flagship AI targeting program has moved from pilot to general issue.

CSTO arms deliveries to Tajikistan. CSTO Secretary General Taalatbek Masadykov said Oct. 21 that Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Belarus will begin delivering weapons and equipment to Tajikistan before the end of this year to strengthen the Tajik-Afghan border. He stressed the program does not threaten Afghanistan (TASS). Separately, India has been selling air defense missiles to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan — a region long supplied by Russia — as New Delhi pushes into Central Asian markets.
sections.whyItMatters: The CSTO border program and India's Central Asian air-defense sales are competing for the same customer base. Moscow's ability to keep arming its southern flank while fighting in Ukraine is a live test of Russian defense-industrial depth.

bottomLine: The Pentagon's two biggest modernization bets — the 2035 fighter fleet and Golden Dome — both rest on a $350 billion reconciliation package that has not passed the Senate, which makes budget politics, not strategy, the deciding variable for U.S. force structure this year. In Europe, the constraint on counter-drone defense shifted visibly from hardware to law: France, Poland and Austria are writing rules for private operators to shoot down drones, and Germany's new threat assessment says no site can be considered out of reach. The through-line is that cheap drones keep dictating expensive responses — 25,000 APKWS kits a year, utility-scale interceptor catalogs, and a Bundeswehr reassessing its entire home posture against a drone that may have sat near an airbase for two years.
sources: Defense News (Air Force 2035 force-structure report; BAE APKWS framework agreement; Reuters-sourced Europe counter-drone investigation; German sabotage threat assessment via WDR/SZ; Golden Dome Army support; NGC2 I Corps funding; Marine Corps Maven; Lyle Goldstein on Chinese assessments of USMC strategy), Air & Space Forces Magazine (Tabor roundtable; Golden Dome funding dispute), Reuters, WDR, Süddeutsche Zeitung, U.S. Department of War, BAE Systems, U.S. State Department, TASS (CSTO Tajikistan), Global Times (Keen Sword 27; PLA reporting dispute), U.S. Naval War College China Maritime Studies Institute, Modern Ships, Shipborne Weapons, SCMP
